questions.question: In an English auction with a continuously rising price, who wins and what does the winner pay?
options: The last bidder remaining wins and pays the price at which the last rival dropped out.
The last bidder remaining wins and pays the price at which she would have dropped out.
The first bidder to drop out wins and pays the price at which she dropped out.
The survivor wins, but she pays the price at which the earliest rival quit.

questions.question: In an English auction the price rises continuously, bidders drop out irreversibly, and the last bidder left wins and pays the price at which the last rival dropped out. What does a strategy of bidder $i$ specify?
options: A single quitting price, chosen before the auction and used for every valuation.
A quitting price for each valuation and each history of observed drop-outs.
A sealed bid for each valuation, submitted once at the start of the auction.
The price at which each rival should drop out, given the rivals' valuations.

questions.question: In an English auction the price rises continuously, bidders drop out irreversibly, and the last bidder left wins and pays the price at which the last rival dropped out. Values $\theta_i$ are private. Which strategy is weakly dominant for bidder $i$?
options: Quit somewhat below $\theta_i$, so that a win always leaves a positive surplus.
Stay active until all rivals have dropped out, whatever the price.
Stay active while the price is below $\theta_i$; quit once it reaches $\theta_i$.
Quit at the expected value of the highest rival valuation.

questions.question: In an English auction the price rises continuously, bidders drop out irreversibly, and the last bidder left wins and pays the price at which the last rival dropped out. Values $\theta_i$ are private. Why can a bidder not lower the price she pays by changing her own quitting point, as long as she still wins?
options: Because it only decides whether she wins; the strongest rival sets the price.
Because the auctioneer fixes the selling price before the auction starts.
Because she pays her own quitting point, which must equal her value.
Because all bidders quit at the same price in equilibrium.

questions.question: In an English auction the price rises continuously, bidders drop out irreversibly, and the last bidder left wins and pays the price at which the last rival dropped out. Values $\theta_i$ are private. During the auction a bidder sees a rival drop out at some price. How should this change her own quitting point?
options: She should quit earlier, since the drop-out signals the object is worth less.
She should stay longer, since fewer rivals make winning more valuable.
Not at all: a rival's drop-out does not change her own value.
She should quit at once, since the remaining rivals have higher values.

questions.question: In an English auction the price rises continuously, bidders drop out irreversibly, and the last bidder left wins and pays the price at which the last rival dropped out. Values $\theta_i$ are private. Every bidder stays in until the price reaches her value. Three bidders have values $30$, $45$ and $80$. What is the winner's payoff?

In an English auction the price rises continuously, bidders drop out irreversibly, and the last bidder left wins and pays the price at which the last rival dropped out. A bidder with value $50$ plans to stay in until $70$. Her strongest rival has value $60$ and quits at $60$; the others quit earlier. What is her payoff?

In an English auction the price rises continuously, bidders drop out irreversibly, and the last bidder left wins and pays the price at which the last rival dropped out. A bidder with value $50$ quits at $40$, while her only remaining rival would quit at $45$. How much does she lose compared with staying in until $50$?

In an English auction the price rises continuously, bidders drop out irreversibly, and the last bidder left wins and pays the price at which the last rival dropped out. Four bidders have i.i.d. values uniform on $[0,1]$, and everyone stays in until the price reaches her value. What is the expected price paid?

In an English auction the price rises continuously, bidders drop out irreversibly, and the last bidder left wins and pays the price at which the last rival dropped out. Two bidders have values i.i.d. uniform on $[0,1]$ and stay in until the price reaches their value. What is the expected payoff of a bidder with value $0.6$?

In an English auction the price rises continuously, bidders drop out irreversibly, and the last bidder left wins and pays the price at which the last rival dropped out. Values $\theta_i$ are private. Every bidder stays in until the price reaches her value. How does the outcome compare with truthful bidding in a second-price sealed-bid auction?
options: Same winner, but the English price is the winner's own value.
Same price, but the English auction may give the object to a lower value.
Different outcomes, since the English auction reveals drop-out information.
Same winner and price: the highest value wins and pays the second-highest value.

questions.question: In an English auction the price rises continuously, bidders drop out irreversibly, and the last bidder left wins and pays the price at which the last rival dropped out. Values $\theta_i$ are private. Staying in until the price reaches $\theta_i$ is weakly but not strictly dominant. What does this mean?
options: It is strictly better than every other rule against every rival behaviour.
It is better than other rules on average over rival values, but worse in some cases.
It is optimal only if the rivals also stay in until their own values.
It is never worse than any other rule, and against some rivals only equally good.

questions.question: In an English auction the price rises continuously, bidders drop out irreversibly, and the last bidder left wins and pays the price at which the last rival dropped out. Values $\theta_i$ are private. What does the weak dominance of staying in until the price reaches $\theta_i$ require?
options: Values uniform on $[0,1]$, since the argument uses the uniform distribution.
Only private values: it holds for any distribution of values and any number of bidders.
Exactly two bidders, since with more bidders the drop-outs reveal information.
Correct beliefs about rival values, so that the bidder can predict the price.

questions.question: In an English auction the price rises continuously, bidders drop out irreversibly, and the last bidder left wins and pays the price at which the last rival dropped out. Two bidders have i.i.d. private values on $[0,1]$ with density $f(\theta)=2\theta$, and each stays in until the price reaches her value. What is the expected price paid?

In an English auction, suppose values are interdependent: each bidder's value depends on the private signals of all bidders. Why can the English auction then differ from a second-price sealed-bid auction only when there are three or more bidders?
options: With two bidders values cannot be interdependent, since each knows only her own signal.
With three or more bidders the price rises faster, so bidders quit earlier.
With two bidders the English auction has no weakly dominant strategy, unlike with three.
With two bidders the first drop-out ends the auction, so nothing is learned in time.

questions.question: In an English auction the price rises continuously, bidders drop out irreversibly, and the last bidder left wins and pays the price at which the last rival dropped out. Two bidders have private values in $[0,1]$. Bidder 1 stays in until the price reaches $1$ and bidder 2 quits at price $0$, whatever their values. Which statement about this profile is correct?
options: It is an equilibrium, but it uses weakly dominated strategies.
It is not an equilibrium, since value-based quitting is weakly dominant.
It is an equilibrium, and it always gives the object to the higher value.
It is not an equilibrium, since bidder 2 gains by staying in until her value.

questions.question: In an English auction the price rises in steps of $10$ $(0,10,20,\dots)$. A bidder stays in at prices below her value and drops out at the first price at or above it; the winner pays the price at which the last rival dropped out. Values are $40$, $55$ and $70$. What price is paid?
